query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of boron during synthesis will strengthen grain boundaries by forming fine, ductile boride phases, thereby increasing the structural integrity of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 without sacrificing its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy produced in its current formulation, which exhibits high applied-field and pressure-field caloric response but shows poor mechanical integrity (cracking under load).
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small, controlled concentration (e.g., 0.1–0.5 at%) of boron into the alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Tested under the same applied magnetic field (<5 T), pressure (<100 MPa), and temperature cycling (across the caloric phase transition temperature) conditions used for the undoped alloy, with standard mechanical loading (compression and fracture tests) at ambient and application-relevant temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, ductile boride phases that segregate at grain boundaries, thereby enhancing intergranular cohesion and reducing crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: Boron, having a low solubility in the matrix, segregates to the grain boundaries during processing and promotes the in situ formation of localized boride phases. These phases increase the fracture toughness and compressive strength by providing additional bonding at the interfaces without interfering with the intrinsic magneto-structural transition that drives the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped material, the boron-doped alloy is expected to exhibit an increase in mechanical measures (e.g., compressive strength and fracture toughness increasing by at least 20–30%) while retaining a caloric response (entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) within approximately 10% of the baseline performance.
generation.baseline: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy without boron doping, which shows high caloric performance but low mechanical integrity.
generation.boundary: The observations are expected to hold as long as the boron content is kept minimal (within 0.1–0.5 at%), under conditions of applied fields, pressures, temperatures that do not exceed the operational limits of the alloy (i.e., typical caloric operational parameters) and mechanical loading rates typical of compressive testing.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal boron concentration and its quantitative impact on both mechanical integrity and caloric performance remain to be determined; there is a possibility that too high a boron level or inappropriate processing could lead to a reduction in the caloric effect or adverse microstructural changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one set as the control (undoped) and the other set doped with an optimized amount (e.g., 0.3 at%) of boron. Ensure that both sets are processed identically apart from the boron addition. Conduct mechanical tests (compressive strength and fracture toughness) as well as caloric measurements (entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) under identical applied magnetic fields, pressure fields, and temperature-cycling conditions.
measurements: Caloric response metrics (entropy change, adiabatic temperature change)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant (≥20–30%) improvement in mechanical integrity (compressive strength and fracture toughness) over the undoped alloy, or if the caloric performance is reduced by more than ~10% relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
